**The Carnival of the Animals**
Saint-Saëns's 1886 "zoological fantasy," a fourteen-movement suite for chamber ensemble with two pianos. It opens with the "Royal March of the Lion" and includes humorous movements such as "Tortoises," "The Elephant," "Kangaroos," "Aquarium," "Pianists," "Fossils," and "The Swan." It is the most common giveaway for him; he suppressed its publication during his lifetime except for "The Swan."

**Danse macabre**
His 1874 symphonic poem set on Halloween night, in which Death summons skeletons from their graves to dance. It opens with a harp plucking a single D twelve times to represent the clock striking midnight, and it quotes the Dies Irae chant in a twisted waltz theme.

**Scordatura violin tritone**
In Danse macabre, the solo violin (representing Death playing his fiddle) has its top E string tuned down a half step to E-flat. This makes it easy to play the opening open-string tritone A–E-flat, the "devil's interval," which sounds like the fiddle being tuned.

**Xylophone skeletons and "Fossils"**
Saint-Saëns used the xylophone to depict rattling bones of dancing skeletons in Danse macabre. He self-parodied that theme in the "Fossils" movement of The Carnival of the Animals, where the xylophone again evokes skeletons, alongside quotations of nursery tunes such as "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star."

**"The Swan"**
The penultimate movement of The Carnival of the Animals, in which a solo cello plays a lyrical melody over rippling accompaniment from the two pianos, depicting a swan gliding on water. It is the most famous movement of the suite and later became the basis for the ballet solo The Dying Swan.

**Samson and Delilah**
His most famous opera (Samson et Dalila, 1877), based on the biblical story from the Book of Judges. Delilah seduces the Israelite hero Samson for the Philistines, and the opera ends with the blinded Samson pulling down the temple of Dagon.

**"Mon cœur s'ouvre à ta voix"**
"My heart opens to your voice," Delilah's seductive mezzo-soprano aria from Samson and Delilah, sung as she tries to learn the secret of Samson's strength. It is one of the most famous mezzo-soprano arias in the repertoire.

**"Bacchanale"**
The orientalist orgiastic dance of the Philistine priests of Dagon in Act III of Samson and Delilah, performed just before Samson brings the temple down. It begins with a solo oboe playing a free, Middle Eastern-sounding melody that descends and ascends ad libitum.

**Introduction and Rondo Capriccioso**
A virtuoso showpiece for violin and orchestra incorporating Spanish dance rhythms, written for and dedicated to the Spanish violinist Pablo de Sarasate. Saint-Saëns also dedicated his Violin Concerto No. 3 in B minor to Sarasate; that concerto opens with a timpani roll followed immediately by the soloist's entrance.

**Piano Concerto No. 5, "Egyptian"**
His last piano concerto (1896), written while he was in Egypt, which he said depicted a sea voyage. Its exotic Andante movement adapts a Nubian love song he heard on the Nile and imitates the sounds of frogs and crickets, while also referencing Javanese gamelan and Arabic music.

**"Aquarium"**
A movement of The Carnival of the Animals in which a glass harmonica (glass armonica, often replaced today by celesta or glockenspiel), flute, and strings play a shimmering slow melody while the two pianos play rippling arpeggios in contrary motion, evoking fish in a tank.

**Organ Symphony**
His Symphony No. 3 in C minor (1886), which prominently features the organ and two pianos. It is laid out in two large movements that still contain the traditional four-movement structure, uses cyclic thematic transformation of a theme related to the Dies Irae, and its Maestoso finale opens with a grand C major organ chord. It was dedicated to the memory of Franz Liszt.

**Piano Concerto No. 2 in G minor**
A concerto that opens with a solo piano cadenza in the style of a Bach fantasia and ends with a whirlwind tarantella finale. This prompted the pianist Zygmunt Stojowski's quip that it "begins with Bach and ends with Offenbach." Its first movement adapts a theme from a Tantum ergo by his student Gabriel Fauré.

**"Tortoises"**
A movement of The Carnival of the Animals in which the strings play Jacques Offenbach's famous "Infernal Galop" (the "Can-Can" from Orpheus in the Underworld) at a comically slow tempo. Other parody movements include "The Elephant," in which a solo double bass plays Berlioz's "Dance of the Sylphs," and "Pianists," which mocks students playing scales.

**Havanaise and Cello Concerto No. 1**
The Havanaise is a work for violin and orchestra based on the rhythm of the Cuban habanera. His Cello Concerto No. 1 in A minor is unusual for being cast in a single continuous movement; his friendship with cellist Jules-Bernard Lasserre also produced the Allegro appassionato for cello.
